title: Visible haematuria and clot retention
subtitle: Stop the clots, then find the cancer

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (NG12)
EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer

red_flags.text: Haematuria with haemodynamic instability or a falling haemoglobin.
Clot retention: suprapubic pain, a palpable bladder, and a catheter that drains little or nothing.
Painless visible haematuria in an adult, especially a smoker or someone with occupational chemical exposure: urothelial cancer until proven otherwise.
Haematuria after pelvic radiotherapy or cyclophosphamide: haemorrhagic cystitis, which can be relentless.
Haematuria with loin pain and a mass, or with a recent renal biopsy or trauma: a renal source.

do_now.text: Clot retention: insert a large-bore three-way haematuria catheter and wash the bladder out by hand with a bladder syringe until the return is clot-free, before starting continuous irrigation.
Run continuous bladder irrigation at a rate that keeps the effluent light pink, and record input and output so that retained irrigant is detected early.
Shocked or bleeding heavily: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol if needed.

assess.text: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet history, and when the last dose was taken. Anticoagulation unmasks pathology; it rarely explains haematuria on its own.
Pattern: initial, terminal or total haematuria; clots and their shape; associated pain or urinary symptoms.
Smoking, occupational exposure, pelvic radiotherapy, recent instrumentation, and travel or residence in schistosomiasis-endemic areas.

investigate.text: Full blood count, renal function, coagulation, group and save, urine culture.

Refer adults meeting national criteria on the urgent suspected cancer pathway: NICE NG12 uses unexplained visible haematuria at 45 years and over, without urinary infection or persisting after its treatment.
Upper tract imaging (CT urography in most adults) and cystoscopy. Every adult with unexplained visible haematuria needs both the bladder and the upper tracts examined.
Do not stop the work-up because an infection or anticoagulant has been found.

resuscitate.text: Review the anticoagulant with the prescribing team: balance the bleeding against the indication, and reverse only for life-threatening bleeding per local protocol.

definitive.text: Clot retention not controlled by washout and irrigation: cystoscopy under anaesthesia, clot evacuation, and diathermy or resection of the bleeding source.
A bladder tumour seen at cystoscopy is resected with detrusor muscle in the specimen for staging.

Refractory haemorrhagic cystitis: escalate through intravesical agents, hyperbaric oxygen for radiation cystitis, selective embolisation of the internal iliac branches, and, rarely, diversion or cystectomy, with specialist input at each step.
Upper tract bleeding (tumour, arteriovenous malformation, post-biopsy) is often best managed by angioembolisation.

escalate.text: Urology on call for clot retention that does not clear with the first washout.
Interventional radiology for persistent upper tract or refractory bladder bleeding.
Senior review for any patient transfused more than once for haematuria.

notes: Irrigation does not clear an established clot. Wash out by hand first, otherwise the irrigation fluid fills the bladder around the clot and you create retention with a full bladder of saline.
A catheter that stops draining during irrigation is an emergency: stop the inflow, check for retention, and wash out. Bladder rupture from over-distension is possible.
The commonest error in haematuria is stopping the investigation at the first plausible explanation: a urine infection, warfarin, or a stone.
